name: Hexoprenaline

lead: Hexoprenaline is a prescription beta-2 agonist used for asthma and, in some countries, to suppress preterm labour.
It shares a drug class with clenbuterol, which is discussed for fat loss, but its documented use is clinical.

paras: It activates beta-2 receptors, relaxing airway and uterine smooth muscle.
Prescription-only, not FDA-approved. Cardiovascular effects such as arrhythmia are noted, and several conditions contraindicate its use in pregnancy.

angle.text: Hexoprenaline is a beta-2 agonist, a class whose better-known members are discussed for fat loss. Hexoprenaline's documented use is medical, in asthma and obstetrics, and no community use for appearance is recorded.

lead: Hexoprenaline is a selective beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist used as a bronchodilator for asthma and, in some countries, as a tocolytic to relax the uterus, with Gynipral the most commonly cited brand [1]. It is a prescription medicine and is not approved by the US FDA [1].

It belongs to the same pharmacological class as beta-2 agonists such as clenbuterol and salbutamol, which is the reason it is filed alongside fat-loss compounds in this wiki's catalogue. No source documents hexoprenaline itself being used for fat loss or physique, and its published use is clinical.
Research on hexoprenaline covers asthma, preterm labour, external cephalic version and obstetric procedures [2][3][4].
infobox: Rx-only; Schedule 4 in Australia; not FDA-approved

paras: Beta-2 agonists act on receptors that also regulate airway smooth muscle, and the best-known members used in body-composition circles, such as clenbuterol, are described as more potent and longer-acting than salbutamol and are used by some bodybuilders during cutting phases.[5] The chain people describe for the class runs from beta-2 receptor stimulation, to raised metabolism and fat mobilisation, to a leaner appearance. Hexoprenaline shares the receptor target but is a short-acting catecholamine, with an oral half-life of about 50 minutes, compared with a clenbuterol half-life that Wikipedia puts at 36 to 48 hours.[1][5]
Hexoprenaline's documented uses are airway disease and obstetrics, and no published report describes it being used for physique goals.

Hexoprenaline is used for asthma, and in countries such as Russia and Switzerland to suppress labour [1]. An early report introduced it as a new bronchodilator in 1972 [6]. A 1977 controlled trial in 20 asthmatic patients found oral hexoprenaline reduced the fall in peak flow after exercise in 16 of them compared with placebo [7].
Wikipedia cites a 1977 review of its pharmacological properties and therapeutic efficacy, with particular reference to asthma, and lists oral tablet and intravenous routes.[1]

Betamimetics as a group reduced the number of women giving birth within 48 hours in a Cochrane review of trials in preterm labour [8]. Hexoprenaline has been compared with ritodrine for tocolysis before external cephalic version, with atosiban in preterm labour, and has been tested to relax the uterus during suprapubic amniocentesis [9][10][11][12].

The Cochrane review of betamimetics for preterm labour assessed 28 trials, 20 of which contributed data. Twelve placebo-controlled trials involving 1,367 women found that betamimetics reduced the number of women giving birth within 48 hours (average risk ratio 0.68).[8] A separate Cochrane review of acute tocolysis for uterine tachysystole or suspected fetal distress included eight studies and 734 women, and a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial compared ritodrine and hexoprenaline before external cephalic version at term.[3][9]

Oral bioavailability is roughly 5 to 11 percent, peak levels occur around 2 hours and the oral half-life is about 50 minutes [1]. Hexoprenaline is not metabolised by MAO or COMT in the way isoproterenol is [13]. Beta blockers reduce its effect, and caffeine and theophylline can increase it [1].

Wikipedia classifies hexoprenaline as a catecholamine and phenylethanolamine, a racemic mixture with the formula C22H32N2O6 (about 420.5 g/mol). Oral bioavailability is about 5 to 11%, peak concentration follows oral dosing at about 2 hours, the oral half-life is about 50 minutes, and the compound is cleared by slow O-methylation through COMT, with about 90% excreted in faeces.[1]

Wikipedia reports that hexoprenaline is metabolised by COMT through slow O-methylation and that roughly 90 percent of an oral dose is excreted in faeces.[1] Interactions listed include beta blockers, which reduce its effect, methylxanthines such as caffeine and theophylline, which increase it, and general anaesthetics and other adrenergic agonists, which may raise arrhythmia risk.[1]

Contraindications for tocolytic use include hyperthyroidism, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, shock and placental abruption, with caution in gestational diabetes; combination with some anaesthetics or other adrenergic agonists can cause arrhythmia [1].

Listed contraindications include hyperthyroidism, cardiovascular disease, hypertension and first-trimester pregnancy; beta blockers reduce its effect and MAO inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants are contraindicated with it.[1]

Hexoprenaline is prescription-only, is Schedule 4 in Australia and is not approved by the US FDA. Wikipedia names Gynipral as the common tocolytic brand and lists use as a tocolytic in countries such as Russia and Switzerland.[1] The oral asthma product was sold as Ipradol in the 1970s trials.[7] Because it belongs to the same beta-2 agonist class as clenbuterol and salbutamol, it is sometimes grouped with them in fat-loss discussions, but its published use is clinical.

Randomised and controlled trials have examined hexoprenaline in asthma, tocolysis for preterm labour and external cephalic version, and obstetric procedures [7][9][10][11][12]. No studies of hexoprenaline for fat loss or body composition were found.

A 1972 report introduced it as a new bronchodilator,[6] and a 1977 controlled trial examined oral hexoprenaline in exercise-induced asthma.[7] A prospective randomised trial compared atosiban with hexoprenaline for acute tocolysis,[10] and a 2022 study compared it with atosiban for preterm labour.[4] A Cochrane-type review of betamimetics for inhibiting preterm labour covers the drug class.[8]
